transcript:
Header:
Date: 2025-03-30
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Sen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood Solutions), Alice Moreno (Peregrine Head of ML), Marcus Liu (Peregrine Platform Eng), Sara Thompson (Peregrine CTO), Ben Carver (Peregrine SRE)

Summary (auto):
Quick catalog walkthrough focused on curation priorities, benchmark selection criteria, and compatibility matrix interpretation. Customer wants guidance on picking open models that balance latency, cost, and accuracy for three different product surfaces (real-time chat, long-form summarization, and vector search embedding ingestion). Discussed hosted vs dedicated, routing fallbacks, quantization impact, and compliance notes (SAML/SSO, SOC2, KMS). Agreed next steps: share bench spreadsheet & schedule pilot.

Topics: curation priorities, bench criteria, compatibility matrix, latency vs cost, dedicated vs hosted, security requirements, next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call? I'll start — Jordan Kim from Redwood. Priya and Liam are with me.
[00:08] Alice Moreno: Hi all, Alice here, head of ML at Peregrine. Marcus and Sara on my side as well.
[00:14] Jordan Kim: Awesome. Agenda — 1) quick context from you on what you care about, 2) we'll walk the model catalog UI and filters, 3) talk about bench criteria and how we interpret the compat matrix, 4) Q&A and next steps. Sound good?
[00:25] Sara Thompson: Yep sounds good. We're mainly here to figure out which open models to prioritize for a pilot — we have three workloads: live chat responses (low latency), weekly report summarization (throughput, long prompt), and embedding generation for search (cost-sensitive).
[00:40] Marcus Liu: And we have infra constraints — want to stay in VPC/private for data residency and need to understand any required kernels for on-prem GPUs.
[00:47] Priya Sen: Great, we'll weave those constraints through the demo. I'll start with the catalog home.
[00:54] Priya Sen: (screen) So this is the catalog. You can filter by task, approximate token length, quantization support, and hardware compatibility. For example — I'm going to filter for "chat-friendly" models with latency under 200ms p50 on A100-40.
[01:10] Ben Carver: Quick question — how accurate are those latency numbers? Are they synthetic or collected from customer workloads?
[01:16] Priya Sen: Good q; they're Redwood-verified lab measurements with common prompt shapes, plus a range of sequence-length profiles. We annotate when they're from short form vs long form. For customer-specific workloads we'd recommend running a short bench using your prompts — the numbers can drift with prompt shape and caching.
[01:28] Jordan Kim: Also note we show kernel mappings and whether a model uses fused attention or requires custom kernels — that comes up for private/on-prem installs.
[01:36] Marcus Liu: That sounds key. Our ops team is worried about needing custom kernel builds.
[01:40] Liam O'Connor: We have a compatibility matrix view that maps model architectures to supported runtimes and recommended quantization profiles. It flags models that have known kernel drift on older CUDA drivers.
[01:50] [01:50] Alice Moreno: Can you show an example for long-form summarization models? We need to know how memory scales and what quantization does to quality.
[01:58] Priya Sen: Sure — filtering to long-seq summarizers. Here's Model A (open-123B) and Model B (condense-11B). The matrix shows memory footprint, p99 latency at 4k tokens, and relative rouge/bleu proxies from our eval harness.
[02:14] Priya Sen: Important note — quantization helps cost but can increase hallucinations in some families; we tag models with a "quant-friendly" score based on our eval prompts. Model B retains 94% of baseline quality at 4-bit quant (avg), while Model A drops to 82% on the same prompts.
[02:32] Sara Thompson: That's helpful. For our report summarization pipeline the fidelity is critical — we can't accept that drop.
[02:38] Jordan Kim: In that case we'll recommend Model B for the summarization pilot, but run a focused regression check using your real prompts as Alice suggested.
[02:45] Marcus Liu: For embeddings — cost per 1M vectors matters. How does the catalog compare embedding generator variants?
[02:53] Priya Sen: We show tokens-per-second and normalized cost per 1k embeddings. There's also a vector-quality proxy — average nearest-neighbor precision on a public semantic search benchmark. For cost-sensitive, smaller quantized models often win, unless you need high-d recall.
[03:10] Ben Carver: Do you support batched embedding requests and caching? We have a streaming ingestion process.
[03:16] Liam O'Connor: Yes — Redwood Optimize suggestions can recommend batching windows and prefix caching for embeddings to reduce calls. For ingestion-heavy workloads we often recommend a small dedicated pool with autoscale and caching layer in front.
[03:28] Alice Moreno: On routing/fallbacks, if our dedicated pool is saturated can you fallback to a hosted replica with same model variant? How does that affect latency SLAs?
[03:38] Jordan Kim: You can set a routing policy: prefer dedicated, fallback to hosted or a lower-cost quantized variant. Fallback will change latency/cost — the console surfaces expected delta. For strict latency SLOs, we recommend reserving burst capacity or pinning to local replicas.
[03:50] Marcus Liu: Any caveats on KV cache and multi-tenant GPUs? We need cache privacy and predictable perf.
[03:57] Priya Sen: KV cache is per-tenant and we have isolation on Dedicated pools. In hosted we do multi-tenant but with logical isolation; for guaranteed perf and cache privacy, Dedicated or Private is the path.
[04:10] Sara Thompson: Security — we need SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs, KMS integration. Do you have docs?
[04:18] Jordan Kim: Yes — we have SOC2 Type II, SAML and SCIM, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. I'll send the security pack. There are also optional audit log exports for Private deployments.
[04:30] Alice Moreno: Great. Back to bench criteria — what do you recommend we include in our pilot bench? Latency p50/p95, throughput, semantic quality, hallucination rate?
[04:40] Priya Sen: Exactly. We usually recommend: p50 and p95 latency for representative prompt lengths, throughput under target concurrency, token-cost-per-response, embedding nearest-neighbor precision, and targeted quality regressions on your critical prompts (pass/fail). Also include cold-cache vs warm-cache behaviour.
[04:56] Marcus Liu: How long does a bench take to get meaningful comparisons? A day? A week?
[05:02] Priya Sen: A basic bench can run in a day if you have sample prompts. More robust runs for p99 and long-form memory characteristics — 3–5 days. For quant/regression checks add another 2–3 days.
[05:14] Ben Carver: For on-prem kernels: do you provide the optimized kernels or guidance to compile them?
[05:20] Liam O'Connor: We provide pre-built kernels for common driver combos, and a build guide for customers with custom stacks. We also flag models that need a non-standard fused op.
[05:31] [05:31] Alice Moreno: Any talk of unit economics — i.e., token cost vs dev effort to keep a quantized model in prod?
[05:38] Jordan Kim: Yup — Redwood Optimize gives estimated cost savings and flags likely quality regressions; you can simulate the net effect before deploying. There's also split-traffic canary to validate.
[05:50] Sara Thompson: Let's capture specifics for our three pilots — what you recommend for each.
[05:55] Jordan Kim: For chat: pick a low-latency model with strong short-form quality, keep it hosted for first pass, then move to Dedicated if latency variance is an issue. For long-form summarization: pick quant-friendly model with strong long-context quality (Model B in demo), run dedicated bench for memory profile. For embeddings: pick a small quantized generator, run a cost vs recall sweep.
[06:18] Marcus Liu: How do you handle upgrades/rollouts? If you pin a model version and Redwood pushes a newer fork, what is the path?
[06:24] Priya Sen: You control pinning and rollouts. Console supports canary, A/B, and automatic fallback; nothing changes unless you flip the rollout. We'll keep version mapping in the catalog.
[06:35] Ben Carver: We have an internal audit requirement for any model that sees PII — what's Redwood's data retention and delete policy?
[06:43] Jordan Kim: Hosted API has configurable retention with options for zero retention. Private/Dedicated keeps logs inside your VPC. We can provide the retention SLA in the security pack.
[06:55] Alice Moreno: Let's talk about the compatibility matrix — I want to understand risk flags.
[07:00] Liam O'Connor: The matrix has risk columns: kernel fragility, quant-sensitivity, long-seq memory pressure, and community support. Each model gets a low/medium/high flag and notes.
[07:12] Alice Moreno: Ok show me where you derive quant-sensitivity.
[07:15] Priya Sen: It's derived from our eval bench: quality delta under 4-bit/8-bit quant vs FP16 across a set of probes (QA, summarization, code). We weight probes per task.
[07:28] [07:28] Sara Thompson: Sounds reasonable. Any gotchas we should warn our infra team about?
[07:33] Marcus Liu: Driver mismatches, odd fused ops, and memory fragmentation on older GPUs.
[07:38] Jordan Kim: We'll include a tailored runbook for your target infra — a short compatibility checklist.
[07:44] Alice Moreno: Perfect. Time check — we have about 10 minutes left. Can we run through an example bench spreadsheet quickly?
[07:50] Priya Sen: Sure — opening the bench template. Columns: prompt ID, prompt text (reference link), expected metric (p50/p95), quality pass/fail, notes. We also include a column for warm vs cold cache.
[08:03] Marcus Liu: For embeddings we want vector dims, batch size, b16 vs quant, and throughput targets.
[08:10] Priya Sen: Noted. After this call I'll attach the template with pre-filled rows for chat, summarization, embedding.
[08:18] Alice Moreno: One last question — competitors. We're also evaluating Anthropic and OpenAI. If Redwood runs a bench side-by-side, can you include those endpoints for apples-to-apples?
[08:28] Jordan Kim: Yes, we can run hybrid benches that compare open models and API providers — cost is on a per-bench basis, and we sanitize credentials. We'll include a comparison column.
[08:38] Sara Thompson: Great. Next steps recap?
[08:40] Jordan Kim: Jordan to send security pack and bench spreadsheet, Priya to prepare a pre-filled bench for your three workloads, Alice to share real prompts and a small test dataset, and we'll schedule a 30-min follow-up to review bench results. Target dates above.
[08:55] Alice Moreno: That's good, thanks everyone.
[08:57] Jordan Kim: Thanks all. We'll follow up by email with the links. Bye.

End of transcript.
